The article is talking about general relativity, you're talking about special relativity. Let's go through this point by point, because you've got most of it, but you're off by a few crucial details.

You've got the concept right that moving fast makes time slow down, that's time dilation from special relativity. What's important to notice though, is that this is due to relative velocity. Someone in the mountains will not see a person at the foot of the mountain move due to the rotation of the Earth. Both are stationary with respect to the ground, which doesn't move appreciably over human timescales. So for special relativity, someone on top of a mountain and at the foot of such a mountain are stationary with respect to each othet and thus share a frame of reference, and will not be time dilated relative to each other.

Things changes when you take a full general relativistic view. While both may share a velocity, they do not share acceleration. Someone at the foot of a mountain is deeper in the Earth's gravity well than someone at the top. There's also gravitational time dilation, which means that time near a massive object moves slower. The stronger the gravitational attraction, the stronger the time dilation. The difference is minute but measurable. So the article is correct, time passes a tiny bit slower on top of a mountain, relative to sea level.

What about someone in a space station, or on the moon? Would the time spent in a (non geosynchronous) space station cause the occupants to experience time dilation?

If so, wouldn't that approximately cancel out the gravity dilation?

And shouldn't this make areas of lower gravity more desirable properties, compared to higher gravity areas (not all of which are mountainous).

Then those two effects are indeed opposite to each other. The ISS experiences slower time than people on the ground due to their velocity, but faster time than people on the ground due to their height. The same with the Moon, though here you also have to factor in the gravitational time dilation effect of the Moon itself.
